title: Constraints composed through meta-annotations

blocks.text: Annotations cannot extend each other (Q6). The page's workarounds are composition: an annotation **annotated with another annotation**, and an element of type `Class<?>` that names the code to run, as in `@Constraint(validatedBy = NotEmptyValidator.class)`.

Given: `Check` (`boolean ok(Object value)`), the meta-annotation `@Constraint(validatedBy)`, the constraints `@NotBlank` and `@Positive` that carry it, and `@Label`, which does not. Write `Checks.failures(Object bean)`: for every field the bean's class declares, and every constraint that applies to it, create the constraint's `validatedBy` class through its no-argument constructor and call `ok(value)`. Return `"<field>: <ConstraintSimpleName>"` for each failure, sorted.

items: A constraint is an annotation whose type carries `@Constraint`. That works for constraints the checker has never heard of.
**Every constraint on a field is checked**, not only the first.
**A composed annotation brings its constraints**: a field annotation that is not a constraint itself applies each constraint on its annotation type (one level deep).

cases.says: @NotBlank, @Positive and a constraint the test declares itself each run the Check class their @Constraint names; @Label, which has no @Constraint, is ignored.
A field carrying @Positive and @Even with value -3 fails both.
@Username, itself annotated with @NotBlank, makes a blank field fail NotBlank.

concepts: Annotations cannot extend each other; meta-annotations and Class-valued elements compose them instead.
